title: You Probably Need More Protein Than the Minimum
hook: The official protein guideline is a floor set to prevent deficiency — not the amount that keeps you strong. A new review argues most people, especially with age, do better with more.
key_points: A review argues current protein guidelines are a minimum to avoid deficiency, not an optimum for staying strong.
More protein, paired with more exercise, may help preserve muscle, strength, and independence as you age.
The aim isn't a 'beach body' — it's healthspan, staying capable for decades longer.
Protein and activity work together; neither does the job alone.
content_html: The recommended daily amount of protein is often treated as a target to hit. But a new review, reported by ScienceDaily, argues that number was set as a floor — the minimum to avoid deficiency — not the amount that keeps you genuinely strong.
extra_html:
The reviewers make the case that doing more exercise and eating more protein than the current minimums can help people stay stronger, sharper, and more independent as they grow older. Importantly, the two go together: protein gives the body the raw material to maintain muscle, and activity — especially strength work — is the signal that tells it to.

The framing matters. The goal here isn't an athletic physique; it's healthspan — the stretch of life spent capable and self-sufficient. Losing muscle and strength is one of the biggest threats to independence in later years, and the review suggests that eating enough protein and staying active, starting well before old age, is one of the most effective things you can do about it. As always, individual needs vary — talk to a clinician or dietitian about the right amount for you, especially if you have kidney concerns.

related.title: Building a Balanced Plate
related.hook: Forget counting every calorie — the simplest healthy-eating tool is a picture of a plate: half produce, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

flashcards.prompt: What are current protein guidelines designed to do — and why might that fall short?
flashcards.back_html: They're set as a minimum to prevent deficiency, not to optimize strength. The review argues that eating more protein — paired with exercise — better supports staying strong and independent as you age.

flashcards.prompt: What's the main goal behind eating more protein as you age, per the review?

choices.text: Extending healthspan — staying strong and independent longer

flashcards.explanation_html: The review frames the goal as healthspan — keeping the ability to fully enjoy life for decades — not appearance, and it pairs protein with more activity rather than replacing it.

flashcards.prompt: The review says extra protein works best when combined with what?

choices.text: More physical activity, especially strength work

flashcards.explanation_html: The review's recommendation is more protein and more exercise together — the two reinforce each other in preserving muscle and function with age.
